articles.title: Researchers Push Over 2 Million Updates to Remotely Disable Popcorn Time Updater That Could Fuel a Botnet
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Between November 2025 and March 2026, the Dutch security firm Eye Security pushed more than 2 million updates to computers it did not own to switch off a background updater that it said could have allowed an outsider to take over the machine.
The updater belongs to Time4Popcorn, an abandoned copy of Popcorn Time, a free app that streamed pirated films and TV over BitTorrent.
Popcorn Time was popular about a decade ago, and the original shut down in 2014, but several copies kept running under the same name. A separate, legal project that took the Popcorn Time name in early 2025 is unrelated to it.
Eye Security, which monitors client networks for threats, found the updater during a routine threat hunt: a program called Updater.exe on one client's laptop kept trying to reach a web address that was no longer registered.
The firm registered the address itself to see what would connect, and about 50 requests a second poured in. It later laid out the operation, which it named Operation IXIM, in a write-up and a talk at Hack.lu on October 22.
Over six months, those requests carried more than 3.8 million different hardware IDs. The IDs proved an unreliable way to count machines, because some Windows PCs shared one and some Macs changed theirs, so Eye revised its estimate to 2.5 to 3 million Windows computers and 250,000 to 350,000 Macs.
The updater ran in the background on Windows and Mac from the moment the computer started. It checked for new versions over an unencrypted connection and installed whatever it was sent, at the highest privilege level, called SYSTEM on Windows and root on Mac, without checking who sent it.
Because the web addresses it called had been abandoned, Eye said, anyone who registered the right one could have served their own program to every machine still calling it.
On a machine with that access, an attacker could install ransomware, steal saved passwords, or pull the computer into a botnet, Eye said. Mapping a sample of the connecting addresses, the firm said it saw home users around the world, as well as machines on government, military, and corporate networks, though it added that it is "hard to draw conclusions" from that.
Eye had disclosed the flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in June. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rates it 9.8 out of 10. It affects three versions of the Time4Popcorn software:
- Windows, up to and including 6.2.1.18
- Mac, up to and including 6.2.1.17
- Android, up to and including 3.5.0.173
Turning the Updater Against Itself
With no company left to fix the software and no patch coming, Eye decided to use the updater against itself. After taking legal advice, it served the machines an update that does one thing: it stops and disables the updater, deleting no files and collecting nothing.
Eye compared the step to Operation Ladybird in 2021, when Dutch police pushed an update to computers infected with the Emotet botnet to disable the malware on them.
The difference, Eye said, is that Emotet's victims never chose to be infected, while Popcorn Time's users installed the app themselves. Still, the firm said, "none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years."
Soon after the updates began, someone uploaded Eye's update to VirusTotal, and antivirus engines started flagging it as malware, a fair description of a program that disables a Windows service. Because every product that blocked it left the vulnerable updater running, Eye reworked the update until only one scanner continued to flag it.
By December 2025, Eye had updated more than 1 million systems and cut the traffic to its web addresses by about 90 percent. By March 1, it was sending about 5,000 updates a day, a 98 percent reduction. Judging the remaining numbers too small to interest a botnet operator, Eye stopped, having sent more than 2 million update downloads in all.
In late March, Eye handed the 15 web addresses it controlled to the Shadowserver Foundation, a non-profit that takes abandoned and malicious domains out of circulation, so a trusted party would hold them rather than Eye.
Public registration records for one of them, popcorntimeupd[.]xyz, now point to Shadowserver's sinkhole servers, with a transfer dated March 20, 2026. Other addresses the updater calls were never Eye's to take and remain with outside owners, the firm said, so machines that reach those are still exposed.
Eye found no sign that anyone else was serving code through the addresses: the ones already registered by other people were parked or up for sale, not pushing updates to the machines calling them. The flaw is not listed in CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 23, 2026.
What Popcorn Time Users Should Do
Switching off the updater does not make the app safe. Eye said Popcorn Time runs on a 2014 browser engine with its security sandbox turned off, loads content over unencrypted connections, and pulls in code from other abandoned web addresses.
Eye registered those abandoned addresses too, which it said would have let it run its own code on every machine that opened the app. It did not, but it built a working proof of concept, so the risk is real. The update only changed the updater, so the rest of the app remains dangerous for anyone who keeps using Popcorn Time.
Eye's advice is to uninstall Popcorn Time. The updater can also be turned off by hand: on Windows with two commands that stop and disable its "Update service," and on a Mac with one that unloads the PT.updd helper. Removing the app is the safer step, because disabling the updater leaves the rest of it in place.
- Windows: sc.exe stop "Update service"
- Windows: sc.exe config "Update service" start= disabled
- Mac: launchctl unload -w /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist
On Android, the updater is built into the app and cannot be turned off on its own, and it installs only if the user taps to accept, so Eye did not send updates to Android devices. Removing the app is the only fix there.
To check a network, defenders can look for the two updater files, Updater.exe on Windows and PT.updd on Mac, and for traffic to the web addresses in Eye's write-up, which lists all 20 domains and the file hashes.
articles.summary:
Dutch security firm Eye Security disabled a dangerous background updater in the abandoned Time4Popcorn app by pushing over 2 million remote updates to vulnerable Windows and Mac computers.

### Key Points
- Eye Security identified a critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in the abandoned Popcorn Time fork known as Time4Popcorn.
- The flaw allowed the software to install unauthorized code at the highest system privilege level via unencrypted connections to expired web domains.
- Between November 2025 and March 2026, Eye Security pushed updates to disable the vulnerable updater on millions of affected devices globally.
- The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) assigned the vulnerability a high severity score of 9.8 out of 10.
- Eye Security transferred control of the hijacked domains to the non-profit Shadowserver Foundation in March 2026 to prevent future exploitation.

### Why it Matters
This operation highlights the significant security risks posed by abandoned software that maintains persistent, high-privilege background processes. While Eye Security successfully mitigated the immediate threat, users remain vulnerable if they continue to run the outdated application, which lacks modern security protections.

articles.title: Critical PHP vulnerabilities force government websites offline
articles.author: Ramon Tomey
articles.content:
Government agencies across Europe, Asia and North America urgently took down websites offline on Wednesday, Oct. 21, after artificial intelligence (AI) tools uncovered critical flaws in the PHP programming language that could affect up to 70% of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by OpenAI's GPT 5.6-Sol AI model and reported to the nonprofit PHP Foundation. They represent a fundamental breach in the foundation of web infrastructure that has existed for decades, but only now become exploitable through advanced AI capabilities.
The PHP Foundation confirmed Wednesday that the flaws were leaked before the intended release date through a combination of mistaken and intentional breaches. Cybersecurity company Chainguard "unilaterally broke the embargo" in an action that "disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure."
Cybersecurity officials across the globe meanwhile issued a coordinated response to the breach. The U.S. National Security Agency (NSA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Cyber Division and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency joined counterparts from the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Germany, Japan and other nations in issuing rare public warnings advising organizations to consider taking systems offline if immediate patching was not possible.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," the NSA wrote in a public statement. "If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated." Thomas Caspers, vice president of the German Federal Office for Information Security, warned that "short-term, large-scale exploitation" was likely before the fix was released.
The two vulnerabilities, dubbed PHP2Shell by researchers, exploit the ability to access parts of computer memory without proper authorization – allowing attackers to remotely run commands on servers running outdated PHP code without requiring a password or legitimate account access. Security firm Wiz, which reported the second vulnerability on Aug. 24, said the findings "rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history." The firm noted that while the underlying flaws had existed for decades, proving they were exploitable required a chain of steps "at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve."
Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reported that exploitation attempts escalated rapidly once the vulnerability became public. "In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," Prince wrote.
Amazon Web Services confirmed the flaw is now "being broadly exploited in the wild" and revealed that suspected hackers attempted to capitalize on the vulnerability days before it was publicly announced. The timing of this crisis is historically significant.
As data loss and information technology security have become serious issues over the past two decades, measures such as encryption, monitoring and password protection have gained increasing importance. Given this, the PHP Foundation warned that "tools now find bugs faster than ever, for defenders and attackers alike, and the number of reports will keep growing."
OpenAI noted in its blog post on the incident that "to our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a defender's window for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure." However, the company acknowledged that while AI can help uncover issues, it can also aid attackers. Indeed, BrightU.AI's Enoch engine points out that AI enables globalists and Big Tech to automate cyberattacks that can dismantle human autonomy and resistance with surgical precision.
Alp Toker, a cybersecurity expert and director at NetBlocks, warned that this incident represents "just the beginning of a wider wave of attacks." Speaking about the vulnerability, Toker explained: "Anybody on the web can essentially access your web server if you're running the PHP software." He added that AI agents could "reproduce the attack much more easily" and cautioned that "these systems are going to continue to get compromised – month after month, year after year."
The PHP Foundation has issued patches for both vulnerabilities and urged anyone administering a website to update their code immediately. As the dust settles on this unprecedented global response, the incident serves as a stark reminder that the digital infrastructure citizens and governments rely upon daily rests on foundations that require constant vigilance and rapid response to emerging threats, with AI now fundamentally altering the balance between those who defend and those who exploit these systems.

### Key Points
- OpenAI’s GPT 5.6-Sol model identified the flaws, which allow unauthorized remote command execution on servers running outdated PHP code.
- The PHP Foundation released emergency patches after the vulnerabilities were prematurely leaked by the cybersecurity firm Chainguard.

articles.title: Logitech Launches ‘Chain Reaction’ to Accelerate Supply Chain Decarbonization towards 2030 Climate Goals
articles.author: Press Release
articles.content:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.
Initiative enables suppliers through renewable energy aggregation and supplier capability building.
LAUSANNE, Switzerland & SAN JOSE, California — Logitech International (SIX: LOGN) (Nasdaq: LOGI) today announced the launch of Chain Reaction, a global supply chain decarbonization program designed to help supply partners cut carbon emissions, optimize factory operations and unlock shared business growth. The initiative marks an expansion of Logitech’s climate strategy, providing direct operational support to help suppliers build their own decarbonization roadmaps while advancing Logitech’s science-based target to halve its Scope 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2030.
Core Pillars of Chain Reaction
Launching with an initial cohort of 17 key suppliers, Chain Reaction delivers collaborative enablement across four pillars:
- Affordable clean energy: Convenes suppliers to aggregate purchasing power and collectively procure high-standard renewable energy instruments. This secures clean electricity at competitive pricing, mitigating long-term volatility and energy risk.
- Energy and greenhouse gas evaluations: Supports supplier-led factory evaluations to identify energy, thermal and mechanical efficiencies. This empowers suppliers to define reduction targets and roadmaps that serve their entire customer base.
- Expert support and guidance: Provides technical workshops, roundtables and innovation sessions, alongside co-developed reporting tools. These are designed to streamline carbon accounting and eliminate administrative overhead.
- Commercial recognition: Integrates carbon transparency and decarbonization into regular business reviews and new business awards, ensuring manufacturing partners gain executive visibility and recognition for measurable carbon reductions.
In fiscal year 2026, Logitech already achieved a 33% reduction in its total Scope 3 carbon footprint compared to its 2021 baseline1. Chain Reaction builds on this momentum by empowering suppliers to identify carbon hotspots and execute practical engineering solutions directly within their facilities and supply chains.
“Real value-chain decarbonization happens directly on the factory floor,” said Elaine Laird, chief people and sustainability officer at Logitech. “Our suppliers understand their operations best. Chain Reaction helps our manufacturing partners access the practical tools, technical evaluations and clean energy solutions they need to optimize their operations and lead their own decarbonization roadmaps.”
To support participating facilities, the program provides technical workshops on establishing GHG baselines, direct access to subject matter experts and pathways to pilot cutting-edge innovations through the Logitech Future Positive Challenge.
“By integrating carbon transparency and decarbonization progress into our commercial metrics, we are enabling more value for our suppliers to grow with Logitech,” said Sree Chenincherry, chief supply chain operations officer at Logitech. “From an operational standpoint, decarbonization and efficiency go hand-in-hand. Equipping our manufacturing partners to reduce energy waste and transition to clean power unlocks structural cost savings, mitigates long-term volatility and strengthens our entire shared value chain.”
About Logitech
Logitech creates design-led, software-enabled hardware solutions that help businesses thrive and bring people together when working, creating and gaming in the age of AI. As the point of connection between people and the digital world, our mission is to extend human potential in work and play, in a way that is good for people and the planet. Founded in 1981, Logitech International is a Swiss public company listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange (LOGN) and on the Nasdaq Global Select Market (LOGI). Find Logitech and its other brands, including Logitech G, at www.logitech.com or company blog.

All other trademarks are the property of their respective owners. For more information about Logitech and its products, visit the company’s website at www.logitech.com.

### Key Points
- Logitech aims to halve its Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 through this new supplier-focused initiative.
- The program aggregates supplier purchasing power to secure affordable, high-standard renewable energy instruments.
- Participating suppliers receive technical workshops, carbon accounting tools, and factory evaluations to identify energy and mechanical efficiencies.

By providing suppliers with technical and financial tools, Logitech aims to lower operational costs and mitigate energy price volatility while meeting its own climate targets.

articles.title: It’s time to find a new browser
articles.author: David Pierce
articles.content:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 149, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy It Actually Feels Like Fall Now At Least In My Neighborhood), and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
It’s time to find a new browser
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Call of Duty is back, Kindle Plus is sort of new, and you need to watch Wildwood.
This week, I’ve been reading about Demis Hassabis and computer chips and permafrost, enjoying the first episodes of Machine Gods,filming the next season of Version History (pet season!), seeing You Can See Everythingand then reading and listening to absolutely everything about it, painstakingly updating all the stuff in my 1Password, making tiny documents with Tiny Little Office, watching Conan O’Brien own Subway Takesthe way he once owned Hot Ones,finally getting properly good at CapCut, and blasting the soundtrack to The Mandalorian and Grogu all workday long.
I also have for you a new AI assistant, the most Duo-y new app for the iPhone Duo, my hunt for the next great browser, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you playing / reading / watching / listening to / modding with Claude this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Obviously, Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest game release of the year, but a new COD is always a big deal. This one doesn’t sound like some grand reinvention of the form, but rather an even more playable, even more powerful version of what works. I was particularly excited to hear that the campaign mode is a huge improvement this time.
- The Blink Mini 4K. Ring cameras get a lot more shine, but Amazon’s cheaper brand also makes some pretty good stuff. This one’s part of a whole new lineup of devices, but $80 for a 4K camera with two-way audio and plenty of smart security features? Not a bad deal.
- JustWatch TV. As streaming services get incessantly more expensive, I’m starting to bail on some paid services and spend more time on the free ones. JustWatch’s new service is surprisingly well-stocked out of the gate — I suspect they’ve been watching what people search for, and making some smart content bets.
- Claude Duet. Here’s Anthropic’s answer to Muse, Instinct, and Dots. Duet seems to be focused on helping you get stuff done at work by making to-do lists, coordinating meetings, and compiling data for you. Still waitlist-only right now, but it’ll be interesting to see if it’s as thirsty for attention as Muse is.
- Wildwood. Before you see this gorgeous, by all accounts excellent stop-motion movie, read everything you can about how it was made. Not a pixel of generative AI in sight, just an unbelievable amount of hard work and human creativity. Humans rock, artists rock, this movie rocks.
- The Teenage Engineering EP-35. When you go to buy this thing, it’s technically called “Life is fantastic!” Which, sure. This thing is a battery powered, multi-input, multi-instrument amp with lots of effects. As always, it is extremely cool-looking. I have no use for it, and I want it quite badly.
- Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. Nintendo basically hasn’t changed the formula here since Wii Sports from two decades ago, and I have absolutely no problem with that. Anything that gives me that super-active tennis and bowling (plus volleyball, boxing, thumb wrestling, and more) is a win in my book.
- Delta 2.0. The next couple of weeks are going to be full of interesting app updates as developers try to figure out what to make of Apple’s foldable phone. But one of the best is already available; Delta can now pretty successfully cosplay as any handheld console ever. (Plus the Sega Genesis!)
- Kindle Plus. This is mostly just a rebranding of Kindle Unlimited, but Amazon put a couple of interesting new features in its $12 monthly reading subscription, including AI-narrated audiobooks. I am dubious of those, but excited about expanding access to audiobooks. We’ll see.
Spotlight
The worst news of the week here in the Installerverse is that Arc is going away. This was obviously coming: The Browser Company bailed on Arc two years ago in favor of the more AI-centric Dia, and Arc has been in maintenance mode ever since. But now it’s not just being ignored, it’s going away. By Christmas, you won’t even be able to use the app anymore.
So now a lot of us are stuck looking for another browser. There are a million new ones out there, many of them somewhere between “heavily inspired by Arc” and “a direct copy of Arc I made in Codex this morning.” I need to test a lot of them. I don’t know exactly where I’ll land yet, but I figured I’d share a bunch of the ones I’m looking at:
- Dia. It has recently gotten a lot of Arc’s best features, and some of the AI stuff is pretty cool. (And mercifully easy to turn off.) The Browser Company’s attention to aesthetic detail remains the best in the biz, so I’m starting here.
- Zen. A total ripoff of Arc, and I mean that as a compliment. Zen runs on Mozilla’s Gecko engine rather than Chromium, which is a win for anyone looking for a little less Google influence in their lives. Last time I tried Zen it was a little buggy and unpolished, but I’ve heard it’s come a long way.
- Orion. I am a dedicated and very happy Kagi user, and I’ve heard good things about how simple and resource-friendly the company’s browser is. Given the seamless Kagi integration, I sort of hope this one wins for me.
- Vivaldi. I used Vivaldi for a while, and I love how customizable it is. I eventually got it set up exactly the way I wanted it. But right next to all that customization is just a feeling of fiddliness, and I couldn’t quite get comfortable in the browser. Might try again.
- Helium. The opposite of Vivaldi, this is a super minimalist, no-frills browser. It’s probably what I need, honestly.
- Firefox. Its confusing stance on AI aside, I like a lot of the recent design and feature choices Firefox has made. I’m also intrigued by some of the Firefox forks, like Waterfox and Floorp, which give it even more customization options.
- Brave. Brave has always felt too heavy to me, and like it’s always trying to convince me to use more of its own proprietary (and often underpowered) features. But it seems to always win in privacy comparisons, so I might need to give it a go again.
On mobile, it’s easy. Quiche is my favorite iOS browser by a mile. Arc was never great on Android, so I’m betting most of us never switched there in the first place.
There are also the default browsers, of course, like Chrome, Safari, and Edge. But each of those browsers continues to fail me in one way or another, and so my search continues. If you’ve found your browser of the future, tell me all about it! Otherwise, I’ll report back here periodically through my journey.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Todoist has a stellar integration with Siri AI that has finally made me fully commit to just using it If you delete Reminders, Todoist becomes the default on Siri AI and you can add a to-do to any project with tag AND location support (using Apple Maps saved locations like home and work!). The best part is that it all works WITHOUT having to say ‘... in todoist’ at the end of each query!” — Sajishnu
“Apple added Sound Glow to existing HomePod models and it’s just kinda fun to watch the light on top of HomePod glow and flash. So I’m doing that with some of my favorite playlists.” — Connor
“I’m reading a book called How to Read a Book by Mortimer J. Adler because I want to get better at analysis and reading for understanding vs. absorbing basic information.” — Rhoades
“My girlfriend took a train ride up the west coast and reported that no less than four different people asked her if her 2024 Samsung Galaxy Z-Flip 6 was the new iPhone Duo.” — Nicholas
“I recently read Bodies of Magic by Freya Marske, and it was excellent. What if med school was magical, but everyone was still sleeping with each other and stressing over student loans? Then an unexpected dead body shows up during finals.” — Emmett
“I got a Framework Laptop 13 Pro running Ubuntu last month, and I’m really happy with it. (I haven’t done anything with Linux in maybe 20 years — it’s come a long way!) So now I’m trying to see if I can replace Capture One with Darktable. If I can, that would break my last tie to macOS, and I’ll replace my iMac with a Framework Desktop.” — Morgan
“Exploring the new Nektropos Castle dungeon in EverQuest Legends. The game has been such a nostalgia trip back to 1999, but new content in an ancient game is a bizarre delight.” — Alex
“Setting up Navidrome and having Claude build me a definitive ‘Songs From the Black Hole’ playlist from my Weezer MP3 collection. (It’s harder than first appears: is ‘Lisa’ track 12 or not!?)” — Micheal
“Best Buy had a pretty insane deal on a Bambu A1 Mini, so we got my 12 year old son a 3D printer for his birthday. It’s amazing how easy it was to put out a seemingly perfectly accurate PLA print, compared to horror stories from older printers.” — Jeff
Signing off
Last week, my wife and I went car shopping. Our plan was just to drive a bunch of cars — we knew we needed something with three rows, and really had no experience with any of them — and then go home. Somehow, a few hours later, we were the proud and slightly bewildered owners of a new Kia Carnival.
So far the car has been great, but wow are there a lot of weird tech ideas in cars now. I’m good with CarPlay and Android Auto. I hate how much everything has become a touchscreen. But I’m most thrown by how many features of my car now exist in a companion app. How do we feel about this? I almost miss when I had no idea what to do about the check engine light.
Anyway, I’m a minivan dad now. I think I’m okay with it. Send car tips! Send minivan tips! Send help! See you next week!
articles.summary:
The Browser Company has announced that the Arc browser will be discontinued by Christmas, prompting users to explore alternatives like Dia, Zen, Orion, and other popular web browsers.

### Key Points
- The Browser Company is shifting focus to its AI-centric browser, Dia, leaving Arc in maintenance mode until its final shutdown.
- Recommended browser alternatives include Zen, Orion, Vivaldi, Helium, Firefox, and Brave, each offering different levels of customization and privacy.
- New product releases featured this week include the Blink Mini 4K camera, the Teenage Engineering EP-35 amp, and the Claude Duet AI assistant.
- Amazon has rebranded Kindle Unlimited to Kindle Plus, introducing new features such as AI-narrated audiobooks for a $12 monthly subscription.
- The stop-motion film *Wildwood* is highlighted for its reliance on traditional human craftsmanship rather than generative AI.

### Why it Matters
The discontinuation of Arc marks a significant shift for power users who favored its unique interface and aesthetic design. As the browser market becomes increasingly crowded with AI-integrated tools, users must navigate a fragmented landscape to find software that balances modern features with privacy and performance.

articles.title: Capcom Data Breach Exposes 11.7 Million Email Addresses
articles.author: Pierluigi Paganini
articles.content:
Japanese gaming company Capcom has disclosed a data breach discovered on October 19 involving its CAPCOM ID service, which provides access to online services and games. As of October 22, attackers stole 11,774,247 email addresses, along with account details including creation dates, last login dates, login counts, and the IP addresses used for the latest logins.
“We have recently discovered that unauthorized access by a third party occurred to our online membership service “CAPCOM ID”
(*1) , resulting in the leakage of some customer information.” reads the company’s notice. “Number of leaked email addresses and system-specific identification information: 11,774,247 (worldwide total)”
In 43 cases, hackers exposed date of birth, gender, country/region, and nickname. Capcom also reported that attackers illegally changed passwords on 196 accounts, and the company has already reset them. The company said the incident exposed personal information belonging to a small number of individuals.
Capcom has activated its incident response procedures and confirmed that services using CAPCOM ID remain operational. The company has notified the relevant authorities, is investigating the breach, and has begun contacting affected customers through a dedicated support channel.
The company also urges users to watch out for phishing attempts involving emails impersonating Capcom or its partners, particularly those containing suspicious links or attachments. It says it will investigate the incident, address the identified causes, and strengthen its security measures to prevent similar breaches.
“In response, we implemented emergency measures and began identifying and addressing the attack method.” states the notice.”A task force was established within the company to gather information and take measures to prevent further damage. The investigation revealed that some customer information registered with “CAPCOM ID” had been leaked. In addition, unauthorized password changes were confirmed for some accounts. On the same day, the incident was reported to the Security Oversight Committee, our external advisory organization.”
Capcom was previously targeted by the Ragnar Locker ransomware gang in November 2020. The attackers claimed to have stolen 1 TB of data, potentially affecting up to 390,000 people.

articles.summary:
Capcom confirmed a significant data breach of its CAPCOM ID service, resulting in the unauthorized exposure of over 11.7 million user email addresses and associated account login information.

### Key Points
- The breach, discovered on October 19, compromised 11,774,247 email addresses and various account metadata including IP addresses and login history.
- Attackers successfully performed unauthorized password changes on 196 accounts, all of which have since been reset by the company.
- Personal details such as dates of birth, gender, and nicknames were exposed for 43 specific user accounts.
- Capcom has notified relevant authorities and established an internal task force to investigate the attack method and strengthen security protocols.
- The company is actively contacting affected users and warning them to remain vigilant against potential phishing attempts impersonating the brand.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the ongoing cybersecurity risks facing major gaming publishers that manage massive databases of sensitive user information. The breach serves as a reminder for users to monitor their accounts for suspicious activity and underscores the necessity for companies to maintain robust defense mechanisms against unauthorized access.

articles.title: Keeping the world safe when no one is in charge
articles.author: Andreas Motzfeldt Kravik
articles.content:
International politics today feels like a collective sleepwalk into the abyss. Three trends are particularly alarming. Artificial intelligence is globalising and turbocharging old and new threats. Meanwhile, no state is strong enough to impose order. And, as in earlier periods of global crisis, geopolitical blocs are hardening, with international cooperation increasingly portrayed as weakness. Alas, there is ample reason to fear a repetition of the worst of history.
Much attention has focused on the risk of war between the US and China, as shifts in hegemonic power historically produce conflict. That is not, however, what is happening. Instead, we are approaching an international order with no hegemon, with several states and regional blocs competing for influence. Using the jargon of international relations theory, we are on the cusp of genuine global multipolarity.
Artificial intelligence is adding further stress to existing power structures. On the one hand, we are all being transformed into godlike figures — soon no innovation or information is beyond our reach. But it is also disempowering everyone, creating new threats and making old ones harder to contain.
Larger states are finding it increasingly difficult to convert power into control. This is already evident in the military domain, where inexpensive drones and AI-assisted targeting have changed traditional hierarchies. The US, with its vast military arsenal, is unable to force an isolated and bankrupt theocracy in Iran to bend the knee; Russia’s failed attempt at subjugating Ukraine is another example of a much more powerful state not getting its way.
New technology is making the loss of control even more evident in other domains. The next pandemic could originate in a hidden laboratory and prove far deadlier than COVID-19. Devastating cyberattacks could be launched from someone’s garage. Frontier AI systems could spiral beyond human control. AI could lower the barriers to developing nuclear weapons, while biological weapons could proliferate without anyone noticing.
Such threats recognise no borders. If one state establishes effective safety measures, nefarious actors will simply move somewhere else and deploy from there. A state can possess overwhelming military and economic capabilities and still be unable to stop a pathogen, prevent a cyberattack or contain the spread of dangerous technologies. Strategies based on peace through strength, regional primacy and zero-sum power dynamics will be like fighting mosquitoes with heavy weaponry — costly and unworkable.
Yet much of the world is doubling down on precisely these strategies. Some state leaders are focusing on winning AI and achieving digital supremacy. Negotiating mutual constraints through international law and institutions is seen as naive or self-defeating. Such approaches are at best ineffective. As global policy, they can destroy humanity. It is as though one can hear the voices of earlier wartime generations: “Do not fall for it again.”
And we really shouldn’t, given how unfettered national ambition coupled with weak international rules and institutions has hurt us in the past. Yet many seem incapable of rising to the occasion. One reason is surely our tendency to underestimate risks that accumulate over time. A 1 percent annual probability of a global catastrophe may sound reassuringly small. Yet, over a century that translates into roughly a 63 percent chance of catastrophe—an intolerable level of risk.
Military strength will remain necessary. But the only way to ensure real security in this new paradigm of multipolarity and artificial intelligence is through powerful international institutions and laws. Global standards must be developed and enforced. International organisations must be allowed to monitor, inspect and report on activities within countries’ borders. Governments will regularly have to share sensitive information. Peace through cooperation must be the new global slogan; not out of altruism but because it is the only way to achieve real security.
Fortunately, we don’t have to start from scratch. Institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the World Health Organization (WHO) still retain unparalleled authority and legitimacy. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has shown that international monitoring can effectively verify compliance even in highly sensitive areas.
Recent events offer some grounds for optimism. Last year, the WHO adopted a Pandemic Agreement, which will improve the world’s collective readiness to prevent and mitigate future health emergencies. The UN General Assembly recently adopted the BBNJ Agreement to protect biodiversity on the high seas, the first global treaty of consequence in at least a decade. The Security Council has shown that it’s serious about addressing the security challenges posed by AI; during a high-profile debate in September this year, most governments and leading AI developers alike called for stronger global governance and more robust international oversight mechanisms.
These are encouraging signs. But overall, states are investing too little in such global frameworks at a time when the opposite is needed.
Norway has made it a priority to break the curve. We have defined respect for international law and effective multilateral institutions as a core national security interest. We’re investing heavily in UN reform; as one of the UN’s largest financial contributors, we have leverage which we will use to push for greater effectiveness. Alone, Norway is too small to change the course of international politics. But through cross-regional coalitions with like-minded countries, we can make a real difference.
One recent example came in September when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb launched a joint Call for Action to establish global oversight and control over advanced AI models. Countries from all over the globe have joined the initiative. Hopefully, it can serve as a springboard for concrete international action in this field.
No one is in charge in a multipolar world. This new reality is taking shape precisely as technology is making threats harder to contain. The defining challenge of our time will therefore be to couple multipolarity with multilateralism. Building effective institutions when no one can impose order is inherently difficult. But just as previous generations were able to overcome profound challenges, so can we.
It was only after the lived catastrophes of the first and second World Wars that nations united around shared legal principles and institutions. I am convinced that, in time, states will once again realise that this is the only way. What remains to be seen, however, is whether we can muster the necessary resolve without first experiencing another global crisis of world-war-like proportions.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
articles.summary:
The rise of global multipolarity and rapid advancements in artificial intelligence are creating unprecedented security risks that traditional military power alone can no longer effectively contain or manage.

### Key Points
- The international order is shifting toward multipolarity, where multiple regional blocs compete for influence without a single dominant hegemon.
- Artificial intelligence and inexpensive drone technology are decentralizing power, making it difficult for even major states to maintain control over security threats.
- Emerging risks, including potential pandemics, cyberattacks, and the proliferation of biological or nuclear weapons, transcend national borders and traditional military defenses.
- International bodies like the UN, WHO, and IAEA provide existing frameworks for global oversight, monitoring, and compliance in sensitive areas.
- Recent initiatives, such as the joint Call for Action on AI oversight by Norway and Finland, aim to build cross-regional coalitions for global governance.

### Why it Matters
The current reliance on zero-sum power dynamics and national military strength is increasingly inadequate for addressing borderless technological and biological threats. Establishing robust international institutions and cooperative legal frameworks is now essential to prevent catastrophic global risks that individual nations cannot mitigate alone.

articles.title: Piero Cipollone: Interview with Milano Finanza
articles.author: European Central Bank
articles.content:
- INTERVIEW
Interview with Milano Finanza
Interview with Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, conducted by Roberto Sommella on 21 October 2026
24 October 2026
Mr Cipollone, you have just attended a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Italian Banking Association. Was the digital euro one of the topics discussed?
We mainly talked about tokenisation. On the subject of the digital euro, I provided an update on the status of the debates on the legislation in Brussels and on the progress of our internal preparations within the Eurosystem.
Since you joined the ECB, payments have become one of the main focus areas of your work. Why are they so important for Europe’s future?
Because payments constitute a strategic infrastructure for Europe and, as a central bank, ensuring the smooth functioning of payment systems falls within our mandate. Whenever we buy something online or pay for a coffee, we think about the price of what we’re buying. But we hardly ever think about how the payment is made. Yet if the payment system stops working, the economy stops working.
Will the introduction of the digital euro help with this?
Yes. Today we can use money issued by the central bank only in the form of cash. But a growing share of our economic life takes place online, where banknotes can’t be used. The digital euro fills this gap. It gives people the freedom to make payments using an instrument that is equivalent to cash in terms of its nature and characteristics, such as privacy and covering all payment needs, but which also works where cash can’t be used.
Why has this now become necessary?
Ever more purchases are being made online. In Italy, for example, according to the latest available data, online payments grew from 6% of the total in 2019 to 24% in 2024. And I expect they’ve grown even more since then.
These online purchases are normally made via card payments and two thirds of these payments are made using non-European card schemes. For most euro area countries, this dependence on non-European operators is not limited to online payments but also extends to physical shops, because they don’t even have anything like Italy’s Bancomat that would enable payments to be made in local shops.
In short, for an essential service like payments, we are heavily dependent on an infrastructure over which we have no direct control.
So can the digital euro be described as a European digital sovereignty project?
The Eurosystem focuses on matters that are closely related to its mandate. And, as I said at the start, the smooth functioning of payment systems is one of our responsibilities. If we are critically dependent on third parties, it’s not easy to ensure this smooth functioning. In recent years Europe has learned that, for some essential services, we cannot rely only on third parties. We saw this with energy and we’re seeing it today with defence. And the same is true for payments.
The digital euro will give Europe an alternative of its own, bringing to the digital world what cash has always ensured: a secure form of public money that protects privacy and is accepted throughout the euro area.
Sovereignty doesn’t mean shutting third parties out. It means having the power to choose and knowing that, for an essential service like payments, Europe can also rely on its own strength.
Does this dependency bring any specific consequences for merchants too?
Yes, particularly for small merchants. Today the fees that a small shop pays can be up to four times higher than those paid by large operators. The digital euro will introduce a European alternative that will increase competition and, thanks to the caps on costs laid down by law, will help to reduce fees for those with less bargaining power.
From this perspective, it seems that there’s no time to waste.
Absolutely. In 2027 we will already launch a pilot based on real transactions carried out by the staff of the ECB and the other national central banks. It will serve to test the technology in real conditions and to build the digital euro hand-in-hand with the market.
36 market operators, of which seven are Italian, are already collaborating in the preparatory works. And we are now calling for e-commerce and mobile commerce operators to take part.
If the regulation is approved this year, the digital euro could be rolled out as early as 2029. When will the final decision be taken?
The decision can only be taken once the legislative negotiations that are under way in Brussels have been concluded. We hope that the regulation will be adopted by the end of the year, enabling the ECB’s Governing Council to issue a formal decision on issuance.
The adoption of the regulation will make it possible to complete the rulebook with the technical rules necessary for the market to prepare ahead of time. The ECB can get the infrastructure ready, but banks, payment system operators and merchants will also need time to adapt their systems and processes.
Will there be a limit on holdings of digital euro?
Yes, but there won’t be limits on payments. The limit applies to how much digital euro I can hold in a digital wallet, not how much I can spend. If a payment exceeds the available balance – when buying a car, for example – it will be possible to take the remainder automatically from the linked current account.
The limit on the amount of digital euro that can be held will safeguard financial stability, particularly in crisis situations. Our analyses show that with a properly calibrated limit, there will be no negative effects on the banking system.
Is it true that it will also work offline?
Yes. It will be possible to make payments in shops during a power cut or in remote and isolated areas where there’s no internet connection or where the connection is weak and sporadic. It will suffice to bring two devices together, as when using a contactless card today. The payment will be made directly between the payor and payee, without going via the internet. It means merchants can keep receiving payments even when other digital payment methods are not available.
This will make the digital euro more resilient and will also better protect privacy. With offline payments, details of the transaction remain exclusively between the payor and the payee, very much like cash payments today.
How exactly will we be able to use the digital euro? Will a new app be available?
There will be two options. Banks will be able to integrate the digital euro into the apps their clients already use, while the Eurosystem will offer an easy-to-use, standardised, reliable app with the basic functions.
Even if you use the latter option, your relationship will nevertheless still be with your own bank; the ECB will not open accounts for people.
But what will this European app be used for?
Just as banknotes are the same throughout the euro area, the digital euro app will also offer a common point of access. The digital euro must be accessible to everyone, regardless of their country, their age or their digital skills. We have incorporated accessibility from the design stage onwards, and have been working with organisations representing those with disabilities.
We are implementing a clear principle set out in the European Commission's legislative proposal, i.e. the choice of how to access and use the digital euro should remain in users’ hands and not be controlled by payment service providers.
Will the ECB decide how much digital euro will be issued, based on a limit set each year, just like it does for banknotes and coins?
No. As is the case for cash, it will be up to citizens and firms to determine the digital euro’s use based on demand.
On which technological platform will the digital euro run?
It will run on a common European infrastructure developed exclusively by European providers, on which banks and private operators will be able to build new services.
We’ve already seen this in our innovation programmes: more than 70 operators worked with the ECB to explore the options the digital euro offers to provide new services to their customers. Some firms have already put forward solutions, such as automatic digital receipts or automatic payment upon delivery for online purchases. These are tangible innovations that will make life easier for people and firms.
We have just launched a second call for new ideas and projects, with the aim of speeding up innovation and creating new growth opportunities for the European payments industry.
Banks have complained because they are afraid of being left out of the digital euro loop. Are their fears justified?
Dialogue with the banking sector has been, and continues to be, an essential component of the project. The digital euro has not been devised as a replacement for banks, but to integrate and strengthen their own payment services. It will in fact be the banks and other authorised intermediaries that will distribute the digital euro, manage customer relationships and develop new services. The digital euro’s common standards will enable payment solutions developed in Europe to reach customers and merchants throughout the euro area.
Is it conceivable that one day there will only be the digital euro?
I don’t think so, and I don’t think that’s what anyone is aiming for. The goal is to create a payment system in which cash, the digital euro and the services already offered by banks coexist in such a way that resilience will be guaranteed and consumers will have freedom of choice.
How can cyberattacks be prevented?
The digital euro’s security will be built on multiple layers: advanced encryption, data segregation and regular testing for simulated attacks. The infrastructure will also be distributed across several European regions to ensure continuity of service even if part of the system were to become temporarily unavailable
Security is not an afterthought, but an integral requirement built into the project from the very start. We can draw on the Eurosystem’s wealth of experience in managing critical infrastructure such as TARGET.
Will we be able to buy everything with the digital euro, such as a coffee, a government bond or even a share?
The digital euro will be a means of payment, not a tool that the ECB will be able to use to tell people how to spend their own money.
People will be able to use it to buy a coffee, shop online, pay a bill or even transfer money to somebody else. In short, the digital euro will be available for in-store, online and person-to-person payments.
The ECB is a federal institution. What is still missing from the European Union for it to become truly complete and stronger from a financial perspective?
Europe already has a single currency and a single central bank. Now we must complete the process through the creation of a genuine European capital market, a more integrated banking system and common infrastructure in strategic sectors.
Today, Europeans' savings far exceed the financing needs of our firms, but a significant portion of those savings ends up outside Europe, while many European firms struggle to find the capital they need to grow, innovate and compete.
We need to find a way of ensuring European savings do more to finance the European economy. A start-up or an innovative small business should be able to access not just capital from its own country but available capital from anywhere in Europe with ease. To achieve this, there is work to be done on several fronts, including legal, regulatory and technological. On the technological front, we have a real opportunity: new technologies such as distributed ledger technologies (DLTs) allow us to overcome the fragmentation of market infrastructures. The Eurosystem is making a concerted effort towards this through the Pontes project, which went live on 21 September 2026. It enables the settlement of financial transactions carried out on DLT platforms using central bank money. Its complementary project, Appia, aims to create a fully integrated European financial ecosystem.
The common theme is the same as for the digital euro: we have a single currency, but in many sectors we still have fragmented national markets and infrastructures. Completing the European capital market would mean that citizens and firms could truly take advantage of the opportunities offered by a market operating on a continental scale.
articles.summary:
The European Central Bank is advancing plans for a digital euro to enhance European payment sovereignty, reduce reliance on non-European providers, and ensure secure, cash-like digital transactions.

### Key Points
- The ECB plans to launch a pilot program in 2027 to test digital euro transactions using real-world conditions with central bank staff.
- A potential rollout of the digital euro could occur as early as 2029, pending legislative approval from Brussels by the end of 2026.
- The digital currency will support offline payments, allowing transactions in remote areas or during power outages without an internet connection.
- To protect financial stability, the ECB will implement holding limits for digital wallets, though there will be no restrictions on total payment amounts.
- The infrastructure will be developed by European providers, with banks and authorized intermediaries managing customer relationships and service distribution.

### Why it Matters
The digital euro represents a strategic effort to secure Europe’s financial autonomy by reducing dependence on foreign payment schemes and lowering transaction costs for merchants. By providing a public, privacy-focused digital alternative to cash, the project aims to modernize the European economy while fostering greater competition and innovation in the digital payments sector.

articles.title: America, You Can’t Get This Powerhouse Phone. It’s a Shame
articles.author: Katie Collins
articles.content:
If the only two names that pop into your head when you think about the best phones on the market are Apple and Samsung, frankly, you’re thinking too small.
Chinese phone-makers aren’t just making phones that rival those from Apple and Samsung; in some respects, they’re surpassing the iPhones and Galaxys — in batteries and fast charging, and especially when it comes to cameras.
On Wednesday, Oppo launched its latest photography-focused high-end phones, the Find X10 and Find X10 Pro, on the sun-bleached Spanish island of Mallorca. A finca covered in bougainvillea and surrounded by gnarled olive groves and roving wild goats might at first glance seem like an offbeat choice for a Chinese tech giant to stage a global launch event, but the decision is far from random. Spain is Oppo’s biggest European market, and it’s only getting bigger.
More from CNET
It’s a story we’re seeing repeat itself around the world. According to researchers Counterpoint and Omdia, Oppo was the fourth-largest phone-maker globally by shipments in the first half of this year. Already well established in China, the company is now seeing growth across the globe, and in Europe in particular.
It’s an impressive feat given that growing a smartphone business is harder than it’s ever been. It’s no secret that RAMageddon, the ongoing memory shortage, is pushing up phone prices and causing a massive drop in shipments.
Phone-makers might be putting on a brave face as they release new devices to the world, but behind the scenes they’re scrambling to draw up new strategies that will hopefully see them through in both the short and long term.
Growing sales of flagship and premium phones will be key to their survival, said Runar Bjorhovde, principal analyst at market research firm Omdia, during a briefing at the Oppo event. Compared with the budget and midrange segments, the high-end segment is relatively resilient.
You might think that means more exciting (if expensive) phones everywhere – witness the launch of Apple’s folding iPhone Duo, which starts at $1,999 – particularly in wealthy countries such as the US. But that’s not exactly the case.
Bad news for US phone buyers
When it comes to premium phone markets, none is larger or more profitable than the US. And yet Oppo and other Chinese smartphone-makers are steering well clear.
There are several reasons for this. Firstly, they don’t have Apple’s and Samsung’s long-standing carrier relationships that would facilitate their phones being presented as solid options to buyers. Together with the geopolitical roadblocks affecting Chinese tech companies, this makes the US simply too tricky and precarious right now to make that investment worthwhile.
“The barriers to enter make it almost impossible to go in and actually scale there unless you have lots of money to invest,” said Bjorhovde. Instead, the money they do have to invest is being poured into Europe. (Oppo said it will increase its investment in its European business by 30% over the next three years.)
This is bad news for Americans, who simply don’t and won’t be able to benefit from the full array of choices on offer to people in Europe and beyond, including the Find X10 Pro. In CNET’s review of the device, Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon described it as “a powerhouse phone that’s well worthy of its flagship title,” praising its cameras as the best on the market alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Xiaomi’s Leitzphone.
Of these three, only one is on sale in the US, but Europeans can take their pick.
“It definitely feels like US consumers are missing out by not having the latest and greatest smartphones from the leading Chinese manufacturers,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. It’s especially noticeable when it comes to some of the cutting-edge foldable phones from companies like Honor, Oppo and Xiaomi, he added.
Breaking the duopoly
The Apple-Samsung duopoly that dominates the American market also exists in Europe, albeit to a lesser extent. But Elvis Zhou, Oppo’s European CEO, wants to see it broken completely.
“People deserve more exciting options,” he said in a briefing with journalists. When it comes to picking a premium phone, he thinks people should have a choice between three or four brands, rather than just two.
This reflects the more diverse array of successful phone brands in China, he added. In his company’s home country, there are only a few percentage points difference between Huawei, Apple, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi and Honor.
Xiaomi, Honor and Vivo are all now vying with Oppo for a slice of the European pie. One sign of intensifying competition is the shrinking gap between products being launched in China and Europe, which has historically spanned months. Zhou says that’s changing — the Find X10 series launched in China only a month ago.
When it comes to choosing a premium phone, Omdia’s research shows that buyers place more importance on camera quality than do people buying budget and midrange devices, but also “softer” values, including preferred brand, perceived status and aesthetics. Oppo has nailed its camera system, but the same isn’t necessarily true of the latter values.
Zhou isn’t worried, though. Oppo is squarely targeting Gen Z with the Find X10 series (Omdia research shows that people under 35 are most likely to buy premium phones), and he thinks they’re savvy enough to look beyond ads to first-person recommendations and chatbots that will provide specs-based advice to discern which product will offer the best value.
“We want to focus on the young generation because … they know how to make the decision very logically – they will not make the decision only following the brand name,” he said. “Young people really care about the product itself, and they can get all the information they want from AI and from social media. It’s a good opportunity for me.”
The company has already found success using this strategy for the Find X9 series, which saw its share of the premium European market quadruple between 2025 and 2026, according to Omdia.
But while Oppo might have made headway in Europe, it might be difficult to sustain this effort over time, said Wood — especially given that all of its Chinese rivals are adopting a very similar strategy at the very same moment.
Competition might be fierce, but Oppo is ready to play the long game. “We’re very patient,” Zhou said with a wry smile. “We’re not rushing here in Europe.”
Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs were covered by Oppo. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
articles.summary:
Oppo has launched its flagship Find X10 and Find X10 Pro smartphones in Europe, signaling a strategic push to challenge the Apple and Samsung market duopoly globally.

### Key Points
- Oppo unveiled the photography-focused Find X10 and Find X10 Pro during a global launch event held in Mallorca, Spain.
- Market research firms Counterpoint and Omdia rank Oppo as the world's fourth-largest smartphone manufacturer by shipment volume.
- The company plans to increase its investment in the European market by 30% over the next three years to capture premium segment growth.
- Chinese manufacturers like Oppo, Xiaomi, and Honor are currently avoiding the US market due to geopolitical barriers and a lack of established carrier partnerships.
- Data shows that Oppo’s premium market share in Europe quadrupled between 2025 and 2026, driven largely by younger consumers prioritizing hardware specs over brand loyalty.

### Why it Matters
The expansion of Chinese smartphone brands into Europe offers consumers more high-end alternatives to the dominant Apple and Samsung devices. However, US buyers remain excluded from these competitive options, highlighting how geopolitical and logistical barriers continue to restrict global consumer choice in the premium mobile market.

articles.title: The best cards in my Google Wallet don't even support Google Wallet
articles.author: Brady Snyder
articles.content:
I've used digital wallets for over a decade. Contactless payments are all but ubiquitous now, and I rarely use physical cards to buy things in the real world — Apple Pay and Google Pay make nearly all my purchases. All my event tickets go into my Apple Wallet and Google Wallet apps. But I've never been able to completely replace my physical wallet.
Support for driver's licenses and state ID cards is still limited, and my state isn't supported by either Apple Wallet or Google Wallet. I have a bunch of loyalty cards, passes, and tickets that don't officially support Google Wallet, too. Digital wallets have features that aim to fill these gaps, like U.S. passport support. However, the feature that finally allowed me to leave my wallet at home was Google Wallet's custom pass creator.
I couldn't leave my wallet at home
Until I started creating custom passes in Google Wallet
By now, most Android users are likely familiar with the process of adding a supported card or pass to the Google Wallet app. Payment cards, like debit and credit cards, can be scanned and automatically added to the Google Wallet app. Transit passes can be supported, too, so long as your transit agency offers Google Wallet integration. It's a similar story for loyalty and gift cards — search your store, sign in to your account or scan a pass, and add it to your Google Wallet.
The issues arise when you try to add a pass to Google Wallet that isn't natively supported. Cards and passes I rely on daily, including my ID, insurance card, and transit pass, don't have Google Wallet compatibility. There's an option in Google Wallet designed specifically for these passes: Everything else. It's open-ended, and that's on purpose.
Google Wallet can use AI to turn anything into a custom pass. You can take a photo, scan a document, or select a screenshot to create a custom Google Wallet pass from the information provided. Open Google Wallet, tap the + icon, and hit Everything else. The camera will open in auto-capture mode, and you also have the option to manually take a photo or pick one from your gallery.
After selecting a photo or scanning a pass, you can crop and rotate it before continuing. This is important, because you'll be able to access the original photo from the Google Wallet app later. Press Next when you're ready, and wait for the pass to process. You'll be able to view a preview of the custom pass and make any necessary changes on the final screen. To finish up, tap Add.
The neat thing about Google Wallet's custom passes is that they work with any type of data. Barcodes and QR codes will be added to the custom pass, and they can be used immediately after the Google Wallet item is created. If there's no barcode or QR code to be found on the pass you're scanning, the information is added as plain text to the custom Google Wallet card.
Google lets you turn anything into a pass
I've added insurance and store loyalty cards to Wallet
Creating a custom pass in Google Wallet is simple, but let's talk about the ways I actually use them. As I mentioned, my state doesn't support digital IDs of any kind. So, I took photos of the front and back of my license, and turned it into a custom Google Wallet pass. It's important to emphasize that this is not a legally valid copy of my government ID, but it's still incredibly useful in my Google Wallet.
I can't show the Google Wallet version of my license during a traffic stop or at a checkpoint, but I can quickly see my license number, issued date, and expiration date straight from my digital wallet. This is handy when filling out forms, both in-person and online. Many of us keep photos of our IDs on our phones anyway, and by creating a private pass in Google Wallet, these photos are automatically password protected.
I added my car insurance card to my Google Wallet for the same reason. It conveniently stores my policy number, issued date, and expiration date on my phone. Plus, it adds my insurance company's phone number to the custom pass, so I don't have to scrounge for the digits in a stressful moment. And because Google Wallet stores the original photo used to create custom passes, I can show it as a legally valid copy in my state.
I've also used custom passes to digitize my frequent flyer number and barcode, as well as my Best Buy Total membership pass. I need that frequent flyer number often while traveling and booking flights, and having it always in my Google Wallet is super convenient. Small passes, like movie theater tickets or loyalty cards, also get added to my Google Wallet.
Don't wait for the 'Add to Google Wallet' button
The best way to build a digital wallet is to make your own passes
It's worth noting that not every pass can be added to Google Wallet. If a pass uses a dynamic QR code, which changes over time to prevent sharing, it can't be turned into a custom Google Wallet pass. If you have a physical card that relies on NFC or RFID, and it's not officially supported by Google Wallet, it won't work either. Generally speaking, if screenshots and photos of a pass work, that pass can be added to Google Wallet.
I spent years envying people who could replace their entire physical wallet with the Google Wallet app until I tried the app's best feature. With custom passes, I can put almost anything into my Google Wallet. It houses information, barcodes, QR codes, and photos securely behind my phone's passcode and biometrics. Now that I've started creating custom passes, I can't live without them.
articles.summary:
Google Wallet’s "Everything else" feature allows users to digitize physical cards and documents by creating custom passes, effectively reducing the need to carry a traditional leather wallet.

### Key Points
- Users can create custom passes by scanning photos, documents, or screenshots of items not natively supported by Google Wallet.
- The feature automatically extracts information from barcodes and QR codes, making them immediately scannable within the app.
- Custom passes are secured behind the user's phone passcode and biometric authentication, providing a private way to store sensitive data.
- The tool is ideal for digitizing insurance cards, loyalty programs, and membership IDs that lack official digital integration.
- Dynamic QR codes and NFC-based cards are not compatible with the custom pass creator, as they require specific hardware or real-time verification.

### Why it Matters
This feature bridges the gap between official digital wallet support and the reality of everyday items that lack native integration. By allowing users to centralize their personal documents securely, Google is significantly increasing the utility and adoption of digital wallets for daily tasks.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Blessing or a Curse?
articles.author: James Mapes
articles.content:
“Generative AI is one of the most exciting and powerful technologies of our time,
but it also presents new challenges and
risks that we need to address thoughtfully and proactively.”
-Sam Altman
Is every great invention a blessing or a curse?
What if one of humanity’s greatest inventions became its biggest threat?
Can something that gives us so much freedom also take it away?
Can technology meant to bring people together actually push them apart?
The truth is that every major technological breakthrough comes with hope. The internal combustion engine promised freedom. Social media promised connection. Now, artificial intelligence promises something even bigger: the chance to expand human intelligence.
History shows us a clear lesson: every big invention has a downside. Cars gave us mobility but also pollution. Social media connected billions, but many people feel more alone than ever. Now, AI is here, offering what once seemed like science fiction. The real question isn’t just what AI can do, but what we decide to do with it.
Here’s the big question: Are we getting smarter because of technology, or are we slowly giving up our ability to think for ourselves?
Take the internal combustion engine. It changed society, gave us more mobility, created wealth, and reshaped daily life. But it also caused pollution, made us rely on fossil fuels, and led to millions of road deaths.
Then social media arrived. Suddenly, we could talk to people anywhere, share ideas right away, and give almost anyone a public voice. But this amazing invention also brought new ways to manipulate, isolate, and mislead people, and created new kinds of addiction.
Now, artificial intelligence is here. It might be the biggest leap forward we’ve ever seen.
My question is: Will AI help us imagine more, or will it replace our imagination? Will it make us more creative or just more dependent? Will it help us understand ourselves better, or just tell us what we want to hear?
The answer depends more on our intentions, imagination, and sense of responsibility than on the technology itself. Does technology make us better, or does it create problems we never saw coming?
Both the internal combustion engine and social media changed the world. They created huge opportunities but also led to results their inventors probably never imagined.
The internal combustion engine.
Here are three negatives:
- Environmental damage. Burning gasoline and diesel releases greenhouse gases and air pollutants, causing climate change, respiratory illness, and environmental degradation.
- Deaths and injuries. Car accidents have become a major cause of preventable death and injury. Technology meant to give us more freedom and also brought serious risks.
- Dependence on fossil fuels. Our world now relies on petroleum, which has led to global conflicts, economic risks, and communities built around highways and cars.
Three positives:
- Freedom and mobility. The automobile gave ordinary people unprecedented independence. People could travel farther, choose where to live, pursue employment opportunities, and explore beyond their immediate communities.
- Economic growth and job creation. The combustion engine helped transform transportation, agriculture, manufacturing, and commerce. It created millions of jobs.
- Greater productivity and access. Tractors revolutionized farming, trucks accelerated the delivery of goods, and motorized emergency vehicles improved access to medical care and disaster response.
The invention of social media:
Here are three negatives:
- Mental health and social comparison. Social media can encourage unhealthy comparisons, anxiety, cyberbullying, and addictive patterns of use. Ironically, a technology created to connect people can often intensify loneliness.
- Fake news, misinformation, and manipulation. False information can spread quickly, manipulate people, deepen political divides, and make it harder to tell what’s true.
On a personal note, my wife and I have become much more cautious about social media. That brings us to the third point.
- Loss of privacy. Our personal information has become valuable to companies. Social media platforms compete for our attention, which can lead to endless scrolling, more distractions, and less time spent with people in person.
Three positives:
- Global connection. People can maintain relationships worldwide, reconnect with old friends, discover communities of shared interests, and communicate instantly, no matter the distance.
- Individuals can share ideas, teach skills, build businesses, and reach enormous audiences without traditional publishers, broadcasters, or other gatekeepers.
- Social awareness and collective action. Social media can expose injustice, organize relief efforts, amplify overlooked voices, and activate communities during emergencies.
After weeks of work, I’ve created a link to artificial intelligence with my new project, ASK JAMES MAPES, which is like a “mini me.” ask.jamesmapes.com
The ASK JAMES MAPES project is a personal example of how AI can help. Instead of just giving out information, it expands your knowledge about imagination, fear, change, human potential, and Quantum Leap Thinking™. It also encourages people to think about their own ideas.
The combustion engine expanded our physical reach.
Social media expanded our social reach.
Artificial intelligence is expanding our intellectual reach.
But each breakthrough comes with a paradox. The same technology that gives us power can also weaken us if we stop taking responsibility for how we use it.
It’s important to distinguish between letting technology think for us and using it to help us think more deeply.
Think about this question:
“Will artificial intelligence become a substitute for human thinking—or the greatest catalyst for human imagination we have ever created?”
My goal is to use AI to help others grow in their lives.
—
