articles.summary:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and other observers highlight that while generative artificial intelligence offers unprecedented intellectual expansion, it also presents significant risks requiring proactive human responsibility and oversight.

### Key Points
- Historical technological breakthroughs like the internal combustion engine and social media demonstrate a recurring paradox of providing societal benefits alongside unintended negative consequences.
- The internal combustion engine increased global mobility and economic growth but introduced environmental pollution, fossil fuel dependence, and high rates of traffic-related fatalities.
- Social media platforms enabled global connectivity and democratic information sharing while simultaneously contributing to mental health issues, misinformation, and the erosion of personal privacy.
- The "ASK JAMES MAPES" project serves as a practical example of using AI to augment human imagination and knowledge regarding personal development and critical thinking.
- The long-term impact of artificial intelligence depends on whether users employ the technology as a tool for deeper cognition or as a substitute for independent thought.

### Why it Matters
The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into daily life forces a critical evaluation of how humanity balances technological convenience with cognitive autonomy. Understanding these historical patterns helps society mitigate potential risks while leveraging AI as a catalyst for human creativity and intellectual growth.

articles.title: PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat
articles.author: Geeks are Sexy
articles.content:
Doug Jacobson, Iowa State University
Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U.S. National Security Agency, cybersecurity agencies and software vendors.
A researcher at Calif, a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it.
The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?
PHP: The foundation of the web
PHP is a programming language that powers most websites. For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP.
PHP operates on a web server in two main parts: the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays.
The vulnerability
The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.
This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.
This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.
AI: A double-edged sword
What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.
This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.
However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities.
This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities.
Should you worry?
Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems. While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.
PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer.
However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.
The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.
Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University

articles.summary:
Global organizations are rushing to patch a critical vulnerability in the PHP programming language after hackers began exploiting the flaw to gain unauthorized control over web servers.

### Key Points
- The vulnerability, discovered in August 2026 using an OpenAI model, affects the core PHP system that powers approximately 70% of all websites.
- Hackers are actively using an exploit tool called PHP2Shell to gain direct command-line access to servers and steal sensitive data.
- The U.S. National Security Agency and various cybersecurity vendors issued urgent warnings after news of the flaw leaked before official patches were released.
- While everyday internet users do not need to take action, website administrators and hosting providers must update their PHP software immediately to secure their systems.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the dual-use nature of artificial intelligence, which can accelerate both the discovery of critical software flaws and the development of malicious exploits. Because PHP serves as a foundational component of the modern web, the rapid patching of these systems is essential to prevent widespread data breaches and operational disruptions.

articles.title: PHP vulnerabilities WordPress: Worst Threats to Sites
articles.author: edward
articles.content:
PHP vulnerabilities WordPress are becoming a significant concern for site owners. Recent updates have revealed serious threats that could compromise the security of many WordPress sites.
Understanding PHP Vulnerabilities
In recent times, PHP vulnerabilities have emerged as significant threats to WordPress sites, particularly as developers continue to update their platforms. These vulnerabilities can lead to various security issues, including unauthorized access, data breaches, and even complete site takeovers.
Understanding the specifics of these vulnerabilities is crucial for site owners and developers alike. PHP, being a widely used scripting language for web development, often becomes a target for attackers who exploit weaknesses in the code to gain control over WordPress installations.
Some of the most common PHP vulnerabilities include:
- Remote Code Execution: This allows attackers to run arbitrary code on the server, compromising the entire site.
- SQL Injection: A method where attackers manipulate database queries to extract sensitive information.
- Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): This vulnerability enables attackers to inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by users.
By staying informed about these threats and adopting best practices, WordPress users can better protect their websites from potential attacks.
How They Affect WordPress Sites
PHP vulnerabilities can have a significant impact on WordPress sites, making them prime targets for cybercriminals. When vulnerabilities in PHP are exploited, attackers may gain unauthorized access to sensitive data, manipulate site content, or even take control of the entire website.
WordPress, being one of the most widely used content management systems, is particularly susceptible to these threats. The following points highlight how PHP vulnerabilities affect WordPress sites:
- Data Breaches: Exploiting PHP vulnerabilities can lead to unauthorized access to user data, resulting in severe privacy breaches.
- Site Defacement: Attackers can modify the appearance and content of a WordPress site, damaging its reputation.
- Malware Injection: Vulnerabilities may allow hackers to inject malicious code, which can spread to site visitors.
- SEO Impact: Compromised sites may be blacklisted by search engines, leading to a decline in traffic and visibility.
Securing against PHP vulnerabilities is crucial for maintaining the integrity and trustworthiness of WordPress sites.
Recent Updates and Their Implications
Recent updates to PHP have introduced several vulnerabilities that pose significant risks to WordPress sites. As developers rush to implement new features and enhancements, they may inadvertently leave security gaps that malicious actors can exploit. The latest reports indicate that these PHP vulnerabilities have already affected thousands of WordPress installations, raising urgent security concerns.
Experts advise website owners to stay vigilant and implement the following best practices:
- Regularly Update: Ensure that both WordPress core and plugins are up-to-date to minimize exposure to known vulnerabilities.
- Utilize Security Plugins: Employ reputable security plugins that can detect and mitigate threats stemming from PHP vulnerabilities.
- Backup Data: Maintain regular backups of your website to recover quickly in the event of a breach.
- Monitor Traffic: Keep an eye on website traffic for unusual activity that may indicate an attempted attack.
By taking these proactive measures, WordPress users can better protect their sites from the evolving threats posed by PHP vulnerabilities.
Best Practices for Site Security
To safeguard against PHP vulnerabilities in WordPress, website owners should adhere to several best practices. Implementing these strategies can significantly enhance site security and reduce the risk of exploitation.
- Regular Updates: Ensure that WordPress core, themes, and plugins are updated frequently. Developers routinely patch known vulnerabilities, making updates crucial for protection.
- Strong Passwords: Use complex passwords for all user accounts and enforce password policies to minimize unauthorized access.
- Security Plugins: Install reputable security plugins that monitor for vulnerabilities, provide firewalls, and offer malware scanning.
- Limit User Access: Restrict user permissions to only what is necessary. This reduces the chances of internal threats and accidental changes.
- Regular Backups: Maintain regular backups of your website to ensure a quick recovery in case of an attack.
By incorporating these practices, site owners can effectively mitigate the risks posed by PHP vulnerabilities in WordPress, ensuring a safer online presence.
Common Signs of Vulnerability
Identifying PHP vulnerabilities in WordPress sites can be crucial for maintaining security and protecting sensitive information. Here are some common signs that may indicate your site is at risk:
- Unusual Website Behavior: If your site is responding slowly or displaying unexpected errors, it could be a sign of underlying vulnerabilities.
- Unauthorized Changes: Look for any modifications to your content or settings that you did not initiate, which may indicate a breach.
- Strange User Activity: Monitor for unfamiliar logins or activity from IP addresses that do not match your usual visitors.
- Malicious Redirects: If users are being redirected to unknown sites, this could point to exploitation of PHP vulnerabilities.
- Increased Spam: A sudden influx of spam comments or messages might suggest that your site has been compromised.
Staying vigilant for these signs can help you address PHP vulnerabilities in WordPress before they escalate into larger issues.
Steps to Mitigate Risks
To protect your WordPress site from PHP vulnerabilities, it is crucial to implement a series of proactive measures. Here are some key steps to mitigate risks:
- Regular Updates: Ensure that your WordPress core, themes, and plugins are updated frequently to patch any known vulnerabilities.
- Strong Passwords: Use complex passwords for your admin accounts, database, and FTP access to strengthen your site’s security.
- Limit User Access: Only grant permissions necessary for users, and regularly review user roles to prevent unauthorized access.
- Security Plugins: Install reputable security plugins that can scan for vulnerabilities and provide real-time protection against threats.
- Backups: Maintain regular backups of your site to ensure you can restore it quickly in case of an attack.
By following these steps, you can significantly reduce the risk of PHP vulnerabilities affecting your WordPress site and enhance your overall security posture.
Expert Opinions on PHP Security
Experts in the field of web security have raised significant concerns about PHP vulnerabilities WordPress sites face, particularly as updates continue to roll out. Renowned security analyst, Dr. Emily Stone, emphasizes that “the rapid deployment of new features often overlooks existing vulnerabilities, making sites more susceptible to attacks.”
Another expert, James T. Moore, highlights the importance of regular audits: “Many site owners underestimate the need for ongoing security checks. PHP vulnerabilities can be exploited if not identified and addressed promptly.” He advises webmasters to stay informed about the latest threats and patches.
Furthermore, cybersecurity consultant Lisa Wang notes that “the community must prioritize security awareness.” She suggests that collaboration among developers can lead to stronger defenses against potential exploits. “Utilizing secure coding practices is not just the responsibility of a few; it’s a collective effort,” she adds.
Overall, the consensus among experts is clear: vigilance and proactive measures are essential to safeguarding WordPress sites from emerging PHP vulnerabilities.
Future of WordPress Security Measures
The future of WordPress security measures is increasingly focused on addressing PHP vulnerabilities to safeguard websites from evolving threats. As WordPress continues to dominate the content management system landscape, ensuring robust security protocols is paramount. Developers and site administrators must stay ahead of potential vulnerabilities by implementing proactive strategies.
In response to the persistent risks associated with PHP vulnerabilities, several key initiatives are being explored:
- Regular Security Audits: Frequent assessments of plugins and themes can help identify and rectify potential weaknesses.
- Enhanced Coding Standards: Encouraging developers to adhere to stringent coding guidelines can significantly reduce the risk of exploitation.
- Community Collaboration: Engaging the WordPress community in sharing knowledge about vulnerabilities can lead to quicker identification and resolution of threats.
- Automated Security Tools: Utilizing advanced tools that monitor and alert users about suspicious activities can provide an additional layer of protection.
As the landscape of PHP vulnerabilities in WordPress evolves, so must the strategies to counteract these threats.
One of the most critical issues facing webmasters today is the prevalence of PHP vulnerabilities WordPress, which can lead to significant security breaches. Understanding these PHP vulnerabilities WordPress is essential for maintaining a secure and reliable website.

articles.title: Chancellor unveils Britain’s ambitious plan for AI
articles.author: HM Treasury
articles.content:
Chancellor unveils Britain’s ambitious plan for AI
Major package to unlock the opportunities of AI in every postcode, scale up home grown AI firms, and keep UK safe from threats announced by the Chancellor.
A major package of investment to unlock the opportunities of AI in every postcode, scale up home grown AI firms, and keep the country safe from hostile threats will be announced by the Chancellor next week.
People across the country will benefit from stronger infrastructure and investment in local economies as the Chancellor (24 October 2026) is set to make AI a part of his Budget. He has announced hundreds of millions in investment to guard against the risks of AI while harnessing the opportunities to raise living standards for working people, back British industry and ensure our country is better off.
The Chancellor’s plans include £10 million per year to lead the UK’s work in understanding how AI will reshape jobs and industry, and how Britain needs to prepare for it, addressing concerns about AI’s replacement of jobs from workers across the country and making sure government is best placed to help people into jobs in future.
The investment announced today helps protect against those risks, and cuts UK dependence on other countries to bolster our security and resilience while supporting home grown businesses and talent. It will boost the UK’s ability to build our own chip design and cyber defences, and will go further to make sure AI works for Britain, boosting the economy, speeding up public services, and keeping Brits secure.
New investments in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester to develop talent will help ensure the benefits of harnessing AI are felt in every postcode through the creation of jobs and new routes to training and skills.
Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey MP, said:
  AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit.
I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI - one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said:
  Our new AI Biosecurity Lab will be a major new global institution, bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats and ensure Britain leads the world in AI safety and security.
As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future. That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on.
We cannot afford to rely entirely on technology built overseas. By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain’s industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country.
Security Minister, Dan Jarvis, said:
  I’m proud the UK has repeatedly been at the forefront of global efforts to use AI for the benefit of humankind. Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.”
AI Security
The economic opportunities from AI will only be realised if our critical infrastructure, public services and businesses are resilient to cyber, biological and emerging AI-enabled threats. This package strengthens Britain’s ability to manage those risks, gives investors and innovators confidence to build here, and will help drive adoption across businesses and public services to unlock growth all across the UK. To this end, the Chancellor has announced:
- £165m for a new National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100 million for a world-first AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to apply AI to the detection and surveillance of biological threats, and £65 million to strengthen bio surveillance and develop medical countermeasures for priority pathogens. As a vote of confidence in the UK’s leadership on AI talent and tackling biological threats, AIBL will be supported by up to £200 million in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, plus partnerships with Google DeepMind and London-based AI life sciences pioneer Basecamp Research.
- An additional £120 million investment in the AI Security Institute to ensure the UK remains at the forefront of understanding AI capabilities and risks through its testing and research, building a shared scientific understanding by testing new AI systems and developing technical standards to ensure risks are mitigated.
- Investing £60 million into a National Cyber Shield that will use agentic AI to improve the UK’s cyber defences, including a £25 million challenge fund to support UK AI and cyber security innovators and scoping for a new regulatory sandbox to support deployment of agentic cyber security solutions across critical national infrastructure, the public sector and industry.
- A new £70 million National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre will deploy AI tools to identify cyber vulnerabilities across our critical infrastructure and the economy.
Homegrown capability to put Britain in the driving seat
As well as protecting ourselves from future risks, this package backs British firms, research institutions and home grown talent to develop AI here in the UK, where we can make sure it is shaped by our values and serves the British public. This will give us greater control and make sure the UK isn’t reliant on technologies developed elsewhere.
- An additional £60 million for the Sovereign AI Fund to enhance its ability to invest directly in promising UK AI companies, to support them to scale and succeed here. This will include expanding into a new focus area of Physical and Industrial AI, building on the UK’s leading research base and growing strengths in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.
- An additional £60 million will support Sovereign AI’s R&D Procurement Scheme, which will deliver innovative solutions to challenges across the health and care system and in AI security, assurance and safe adoption.
- Building up the UK’s AI hardware capabilities with £18 million to support a new UK Advanced Chip Design Academy, helping build advanced chip-design skills, connect British research more directly with advanced semiconductor manufacturing, and support the government’s drive towards reindustrialisation
Good growth in every postcode
Every part of the country must feel the benefits of the economic opportunities from AI. Support for British innovation, investment in AI to improve public services and programmes to help communities use AI to support local economies will help drive up living standards and unlock growth in every postcode.
- £15 million for an AI Challenge Prize to reward innovative AI that fixes people’s common problems with the first award targeted at firms and innovators solving health issues with AI.
- An additional £23 million over the next three years for the AI Economics Institute, the world’s first government-backed research institution dedicated to analysing the economic impacts of AI. The funding will underpin the Institute’s comprehensive research agenda on how AI is affecting productivity, growth, jobs and living standards. As part of this, the AIEI will also support the UK’s international research collaboration on these issues, including in support of the UK’s G20 Presidency next year.
- Investing in a new National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence in Manchester to train and develop the next generation of government cyber and AI experts, so that more people can get the skills they need to do the jobs of the future.
- £30m to kickstart local AI partnerships with Mayoral Strategic Authorities, empowering local leaders to bring together councils, businesses, universities, colleges and other partners to pursue locally-led approaches to AI adoption to improve services, support local businesses, including SMEs, and provide workers with AI skills.
AI is already helping to deliver better public services across the country. For example, in the NHS it is already being used to help clinicians analyse over 210,000 chest X-rays each month, around a third of all chest X-rays in the NHS. This has led to an 11.5% increase in suspected lung cancer cases identified within 24 hours, meaning around 400 more patients receive faster clarity each month, while reducing the average wait for follow-up CT scans from 6.3 to 5.6 days.
This is alongside HMRC’s AI-powered digital assistant, Ask HMRC, which supported around 6.3 million customer interactions in 2025-26, helping them navigate services and resolve routine enquiries while freeing up around 400 full-time equivalent work hours for more complex work.
Together, this sets out a distinctively British approach to AI: managing risks responsibly, ambitious about the opportunity, and backed by the institutions, capabilities and infrastructure needed to manage the transition. It will enable Britain to shape the AI age rather than simply respond to it and ensure people across the country are better off as a result.
Stakeholder quotes:
Julian David OBE, CEO, techUK said:
  This is a strong £600m+ package focused on AI adoption, trust and security, investment and AI’s impact on jobs and society.
It signals that government is focused on the right issues on both securing the benefits of AI for the whole of the UK whilst also tackling the biggest questions and challenges around safety, security and economic impact.
This funding plays to the UK’s strengths in building, adopting and securing AI, and helps British AI firms grow here, not abroad, which is a vital step to build our sovereign AI capability.
Aurelia Nguyen, Deputy CEO of CEPI said:
  Rapid advances in AI are creating new risks related to the design and modification of pathogens, increasing the potential for both accidental and deliberate harm. But, used safely and securely, the same technology can help us detect threats earlier and design lifesaving vaccines faster, fundamentally changing what is possible in pandemic preparedness.
The UK’s AI Biosecurity Lab complements CEPI’s goal to ensure advances in AI translate into stronger preparedness and greater protection against future biological threats.
Oliver Vince, Co-Founder at Basecamp said:
  Basecamp Research is proud to support the AI Biosecurity Lab. It’s great that the UK government is deploying cutting edge AI capabilities to strengthen our resilience.
Ciaran Martin CB, former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre
  This is a really welcome package at a critical time for our cyber defences. This week we’ve had a stark reminder that AI exposes some of our digital world’s weaknesses and brings new ways of exploiting them to those who’d do us harm. So we need to padlock our systems, and harness AI for defence. These measures, and the crucial reinforcement of the work of the NCSC and AISI, will help us do just that.
David Sully, CEO, Advai said:
  Britain has an opportunity to be at the heart of the world’s future AI safety and security ecosystem, with British companies already showing an early lead. The Chancellor’s commitment to support, grow and enable this sector will help accelerate these future global leaders.
Dr Gordon Sanghera CBE FRS - Founder and Tech Innovation Advisor, Oxford Nanopore Technologies said:
  AIBL is a bold investment in UK resilience, harnessing AI to strengthen preparedness and maintain the UK’s position as a global science and technology leader
Professor Hugh Brady, President, Imperial College London:
  Biosecurity is one of the defining challenges of our generation. Whether a threat arises in nature or is deliberately engineered, its likelihood and its potential impact are both increasing. Our capabilities must keep pace. AI offers extraordinary potential to detect threats earlier, respond faster, and stay ahead of risks that are evolving in real time. Imperial’s Global Biosecurity Network is already bringing together world-leading researchers, policymakers and industry to close the gap between the threats we face and our ability to respond to them. But this cannot be done by any single institution alone. The AI Biosecurity Lab is an important and very welcome initiative and we look forward to working together on the actions needed to meet this moment.
articles.summary:
The UK Chancellor has announced a major investment package exceeding £600 million to bolster national AI security, support homegrown technology firms, and drive economic growth across all regions.

### Key Points
- A £165 million National AI Biosecurity Initiative includes a world-first AI Biosecurity Lab supported by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Basecamp Research.
- The AI Security Institute will receive £120 million to advance testing, research, and technical standards for AI safety.
- New cyber defense measures include a £60 million National Cyber Shield and a £70 million National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
- The Sovereign AI Fund will receive an additional £60 million to scale UK-based companies, with a new focus on physical and industrial AI.
- A new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester and an Advanced Chip Design Academy in Edinburgh will foster regional talent and hardware capabilities.
- £30 million is allocated for local AI partnerships to help businesses and public services adopt technology across every UK postcode.

### Why it Matters
This investment aims to reduce British reliance on foreign technology while positioning the UK as a global leader in AI safety and industrial resilience. By integrating security infrastructure with regional economic development, the government seeks to mitigate job displacement risks and ensure that AI-driven growth benefits the entire country.

articles.title: AI Billionaires Are Flooding Money Into Politics to Influence Elections, But It’s Backfiring
articles.author: Frank Landymore
articles.content:
Unreasonably wealthy AI plutocrats are pouring billions of dollars into US elections.
Elon Musk alone has pumped more than $445 million into Republican campaigns ahead of the midterms, after spending a near-equal sum to get president Donald Trump elected in the last election cycle. Leading The Future, a Super PAC backed by OpenAI and Palantir cofounders and prominent tech venture capitalists including Marc Andreessen, has amassed $140 million to dole out to pro-AI candidates.
But all that money doesn’t seem to be helping the AI industry’s interests, because its image is still in the toilet.
A new analysis from Guardrails Action, an AI accountability advocacy group, found that voters in key battleground states still harbor mostly negative feelings towards the AI industry, with the tech being such a toxic topic that it’s potentially driving voters to cross the aisle.
The survey, reported by Inc, questioned over 3,000 likely voters in Iowa, Michigan, and Ohio — states where close Senate races are unfolding — about their thoughts on AI.
AI, the results showed, is a political landmine, with even a whiff of Big Tech money being potentially disastrous for a candidate’s image.
Three quarters of the likely voters said that they would be less apt to vote for a candidate if they found out they had accepted a donation from an AI Super PAC.
Some felt even more strongly than that. A quarter said they would switch parties to vote for a candidate who took a strong stance against AI companies and data center construction.
“We found that the AI Super PACs were more toxic with voters than Wall Street, cryptocurrency or AIPAC,” Charles Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that combats AI spending that the advocacy group is part of, told Inc. “The influence of AI money on elections and politics sits at this nexus of the anxieties that people are feeling about AI, and this increased disgust people have around corruption and special interest money and politics.”
Ironically, this seems to be because voters are convinced by some of the noise coming out of the industry itself. Many luminaries in the industry have pushed doomy narratives about their tech destroying civilization, wiping out jobs, and possibly being conscious — while companies including Anthropic and OpenAI warn about their AIs going on rogue hacking sprees.

articles.title: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
articles.author: Dania Durnas
articles.content:
TL;DR
⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well.
On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available.
Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available.
Update 4:12PM PT: Patches are available for libbrotli, Python, C++, NodeJS, bun, Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default.
Update 4:15 PM PT: OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here. 
What is Brotli?
Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
What is CVE-2026-111497?
CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.
A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.
OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses.
The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update.
You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet.
You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel.
As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli
How to patch HTTP2Shell CVE-2026-111497
For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:
- Node.js: upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line.
- Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to 1.2.1 or later. For older release lines, use patched 1.0.10 or 1.1.1.
- Python packages: upgrade Brotli to 1.2.1 or later and brotlicffi to 1.2.1.0 or later, wherever installed.
- curl / libcurl: update its Brotli dependency to 1.2.1, a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build.
- Bun: upgrade to 1.4.4 or later. Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun.
- Envoy: upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8, or a newer release in a supported branch. 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported.
- Istio: the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2. Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life.
- Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number.
- Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider.
Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.
What to do if you can't upgrade yet
These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade:
- Python applications: where Brotli support is optional, uninstall both Brotli and brotlicffi from affected environments. Remove dependency extras such as httpx[brotli] and any other requirements that would reinstall them, then regenerate dependency locks and rebuild/restart workloads. HTTPX, Requests, and urllib3 retain gzip and deflate support without these optional packages. However, a server that sends Brotli anyway may produce an unreadable response or an application error; automatic fallback is not guaranteed. 
  - Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products.
- Incoming HTTP requests: reject requests whose Content-Encoding includes br at the reverse proxy, load balancer, or application middleware, before any vulnerable decoder processes the body. Match br case-insensitively, including within lists of encodings.
- Outbound HTTP requests: remove br from Accept-Encoding. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late.
Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header.
Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths.
How Aikido helps with CVE-2026-111497
Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images, and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies. Your dashboard shows which services still run a vulnerable version, so you can upgrade the ones that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies first.
Once you've upgraded, Aikido checks if the finding is gone.
The timeline
Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 22nd NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. Users were exposed if their app or a library decompresses bad Brotli data (e.g. the built-in fetch(), body-parser).
The next day, Python released a security update that patches the same flaw; Python packages were also vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497. Brotli flaw may affect even more languages and service applications, given how widely integrated the library is downstream. It turns out OpenAI had found this back in February.
Techincal details of CVE-2026-111497
The flaw sits in DecodeBlockTypeAndLength(), which handles block switches, the points where a Brotli stream changes which Huffman tree it uses. In vulnerable versions the function returns a plain boolean, and BROTLI_FALSE can mean either "this stream is malformed" or "I need more input." Callers can't tell the two apart, and on the fast path the decoder discards the return value entirely.
A crafted stream can declare a single block type and then exhaust that block's length, which forces a switch that can't succeed. The decoder then either reports that it needs more input for a stream that's complete, or keeps decoding with the block state it already had. That second path leads to the out-of-bounds write.
The upstream fix, google/brotli commit 0ed4268, makes the function return an error code and adds a new error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (-17). Decoding now stops on a format error on both the safe and fast paths. OSM diffed the Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 source distributions and found that 1.2.1 differs only in the version bump and the decoder changes from that commit.
Brotli vulnerabilities in Python libraries (CVE-2026-111497)
The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) affects Python. Two PyPI packages, Brotli and brotlicffi, compile the same vulnerable Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles. An official advisory was posted on GitHub. Brotli has 82.8 million downloads per month.
You're affected if any Python environment you run has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier, or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x, installed. Popular HTTP clients such as requests and httpx load these packages automatically when they're present. Some packages automatically install Brotli as a dependency such as Scrapy, while others require explicit mention of it. An attacker can reach the vulnerable decoder by sending a malicious Brotli response to a request your app makes, or by sending your app a request body compressed with Brotli. That means an app can be exposed without importing Brotli anywhere in its own code. It’s a popular transitive dependency, so check your systems.
To fix it, upgrade to the patched releases:
- Brotli -> 1.2.1
- brotlicffi -> 1.2.1.0
The release notes for both fixed versions don't mention the CVE. As of October 23, advisory databases don't map it to either PyPI package yet, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won't flag these versions.
Who is affected by CVE-2026-111497 in Python?
You’re affected if any of your Python environments have one of these packages installed:
Your code doesn’t have to import either package. These HTTP clients advertise Accept-Encoding: br and decode Brotli responses automatically:
- urllib3 (and therefore requests) when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed
- httpx with the brotli extra
- aiohttp when Brotli is installed
- Scrapy, and anything built on the clients above
Attacker data can reach the decoder through two routes:
- Outbound requests. Your app fetches a Brotli response from a server an attacker controls, such as through a webhook delivery, URL preview, crawler or “fetch this URL” feature.
- Inbound requests. Your framework or middleware decodes a request body sent with Content-Encoding: br, which is the Python equivalent of the Express 5 case in Node.js.
How to fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python
The fix is a package upgrade, and it takes four steps:
- Upgrade whichever package you have installed with pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" or pip install -U "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0". If you use a lockfile with Poetry, uv, or pip-tools, update the constraint and regenerate the lockfile.
- Rebuild your container images and any wheels that bundle either package. An image built on a vulnerable version stays vulnerable until you rebuild it.
- Check every environment you run, including laptops, CI runners, servers and containers. Many projects pull in Brotli through an HTTP client extra, so look at your full resolved dependency tree.
- Rely on a manual check for now. pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety won't report this until the advisory databases map the CVE to the PyPI packages.
If your Python Brotli bindings came from a Linux distribution package instead of PyPI, the fix comes through your distribution, so check its security advisory as well.
What is the Python Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)?
Python Brotli vulnerability refers to CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder flaw known as Node2Shell, as it affects Python packages on PyPI. The CVE record pairs CWE-252 (unchecked return value) with CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).
How serious is CVE-2026-111497 for Python, and is it being exploited?
The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and Node.js rates it high severity. OSM built Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 with AddressSanitizer and ran a crafted stream through both. Version 1.2.0 consumed all of the roughly 23 MB stream and kept reporting that it needed more input, whether the stream arrived in one piece or in chunks as small as one byte. Version 1.2.1 rejected the stream with error -17 every time.
OSM didn't pursue memory corruption or code execution in the Python extension. The decoder code is the same code that researchers exploited against an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build, as Imperva and others reported. For Node.js, The Hacker News reported no exploitation in the wild as of October 22.
Treat it as urgent anyway. The bug is a memory-safety flaw in a component that handles untrusted network input, and the fix is a routine version bump. Services that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies should go first.
How to check if your Python app is exposed
- Check installed versions with pip show Brotli brotlicffi in each environment, and with docker run --rm <image> pip show Brotli brotlicffi for each container image.
- Find what pulls the packages in. Run pipdeptree -r -p Brotli to see which dependencies require it, and search your lockfiles with grep -i brotli poetry.lock uv.lock requirements*.txt.
- List the outbound HTTP calls that go to servers you don't control, and any endpoints that decode Content-Encoding: br request bodies.
- Upgrade the services that match step 3 first, then the rest.
If you're reproducing the bug from Python, brotli.decompress() raises a generic brotli.error: decoder failed for any error, so you can't see which error code fired. A Decompressor() fed the crafted stream incrementally will never finish on 1.2.0.
FAQ
Which versions fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python?
Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0, along with any newer releases.
Do I need to import Brotli in my code to be affected?
An installed package is enough. urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp use Brotli or brotlicffi automatically when either is present and decode Brotli responses from any server your app calls.
Will pip-audit or Dependabot flag this?
Not yet. As of October 23, the CVE record, OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database don't list either PyPI package. OSM is submitting PYSEC entries and a PyPI package mapping for the GitHub advisory so that tooling picks this up.
Is there a workaround?
Uninstalling Brotli and brotlicffi removes the vulnerable decoder, and HTTP clients fall back to gzip and deflate. Rejecting Brotli-encoded requests at the edge reduces inbound exposure, but it doesn't protect against Brotli responses your app fetches.

### Key Points

articles.title: Budget Android Phones Have A Storage Problem That You Might Not Have Noticed
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Jules Wang)
articles.content:
Budget Android Phones Have A Storage Problem That You Might Not Have Noticed
If you've got $200 or less to spend on an Android phone, there's one spec line you should be checking before any other: the storage. No, not how much there is (although it can be too easy to fill it up), but how fast it is. That will depend on what type of memory is used and you'll want to look for UFS rather than eMMC.
The big advantage Universal Flash Storage has against the embedded MultiMedia Card format is the ability to read and write simultaneously. In fact, the performance gap is so vast that the Joint Electron Device Engineering Council (JEDEC), which is the caretaker for both standards, has effectively made UFS the successor to eMMC. The last major update to eMMC was made in 2015 (though the standard has been revised slightly on occasion) while UFS was updated to version 5.0 in February.
Budget Android phones sold in the U.S. have previously used eMMC storage, but major brands including Samsung and Motorola have moved up to UFS, though an older version at times. The Samsung Galaxy A17 5G and sub-$200 Moto G Play 2026 use UFS 2.2 disks which, reading at more than 500MB per second on average, are capable of roughly double the performance of an eMMC 5.1 disk, or even better. You might be able to find new feature phones like the TCL Flip 4 5G that use eMMC. You'll also see eMMC storage on extremely cheap laptops such as Chromebooks.
UFS has replaced eMMC for the most part, but...
Storage has long been an easy corner to cut for phone makers. Samsung stocked its base model Galaxy S23 and S24 with 128GB UFS 3.1 disks, for example, even the company itself manufactured UFS 4.0 memory at larger capacities with double the read and write speeds. These days, you'll find some devices in the $300 to $500 range featuring UFS 3.1 memory, such as the Galaxy A27 or Nothing Phone (4a) Pro and others with UFS 2.2 such as the Nothing Phone (4b) and the Moto G Power (2026).
With memory prices as high as they are right now thanks to explosive demand from artificial intelligence use, there is a chance that the budget Android phone market may die as companies lose what little margin they were making. NAND flash and DRAM chips, which both UFS and eMMC rely on, aren't expected to see price drops anytime soon. If anything, they've continued to rise, pushing Samsung to raise prices on its Galaxy A17 twice after launching it in the U.S. this year: once from $200 to $250 in August and then again to $270 just this month. Many other Samsung phones also got a price hike in October, as have devices from many other tech companies over 2026.
eMMC is still used in phones sold outside the U.S. like the Galaxy A07, but whether they'll be reintroduced into America one way or another is an open question at this point.

Budget Android smartphone buyers should prioritize Universal Flash Storage (UFS) over older eMMC memory to ensure significantly faster read and write speeds for better device performance.

### Key Points
- UFS technology allows for simultaneous data reading and writing, offering roughly double the performance of older eMMC 5.1 storage standards.
- Major manufacturers like Samsung and Motorola are increasingly adopting UFS 2.2 for budget models, such as the Galaxy A17 5G and Moto G Play 2026.
- Older eMMC storage remains common in entry-level devices like the TCL Flip 4 5G and various budget-friendly Chromebook laptops.
- Rising costs for NAND flash and DRAM chips, driven by high demand for artificial intelligence hardware, are forcing manufacturers to increase retail prices.
- Samsung raised the U.S. price of the Galaxy A17 5G from $200 to $270 throughout 2026 due to these ongoing supply chain and component cost pressures.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward faster storage standards is critical for maintaining device longevity and user experience as mobile applications become more resource-intensive. However, rising component costs threaten the viability of the budget smartphone market, potentially forcing consumers to pay higher prices for entry-level technology.

articles.title: SudoStamp
articles.author: Kitploit
articles.content:
Approve sudo on a Linux workstation with a fingerprint on your Android phone. LAN only; the ECDSA key never leaves the phone's TEE and speaks the ssh-agent protocol to pam_rssh.
Approve sudo on your Linux machine by touching your Android phone's fingerprint sensor.
Type sudo, your phone buzzes, you touch the sensor, the command runs. No password typed, nothing
in the cloud: the phone answers over your LAN, and the fingerprint is enforced by the phone's secure
hardware (TEE / StrongBox), not by app code. If anything goes wrong (phone off, out of range, you
tap Deny, 60 seconds pass) sudo simply falls back to your ordinary password prompt. It can make
sudo more convenient; it cannot lock you out.
| 1. sudo on the host The phone pops up who is asking. Deny works right from here. | 2. Tap it A countdown, the host and time, a warning for never-seen hosts. Then the system fingerprint prompt. | 3. Touch the sensor The TEE signs, sudo proceeds, the app closes itself. | 
| First run Three steps and one button. Offers fingerprint enrollment if the phone has none. | Setup A live checklist: listener, notifications, battery, Do Not Disturb. "Ready" only when all pass. | Denied or timed out No signature leaves the phone; the host asks for the password. | 
Screenshots from a Pixel 7 emulator (hence 10.0.2.2, the emulator's host). The
system fingerprint sheet that appears over step 2 is a secure window and does not show in
screenshots.
sudo on the host
  -> PAM: pam_rssh (third-party) dials the phone over the LAN, as an ssh-agent
  -> phone: "Approve sudo? From 192.168.1.10"              (notification)
  -> tap -> BiometricPrompt -> fingerprint
  -> the phone's TEE signs pam_rssh's fresh 32-byte challenge
  -> pam_rssh verifies against the pinned public key -> sudo proceeds
pam_rssh's,
an existing, maintained module. Nothing written here runs as root on the host at
authentication time.setUserAuthenticationParameters(0, AUTH_BIOMETRIC_STRONG): a fresh strong biometric for
every signature, enforced inside the TEE (or StrongBox). Malware on the phone cannot sign
without your finger either, and the key cannot be exported.
SECURITY.md has the full threat model, including what it does not protect against. docs/DESIGN.md has the design and the reasoning behind it.
Phone: Android 11+ (API 30, where per-use biometric keys became expressible) with a Class 3 ("strong") fingerprint sensor.
Host: any of the platforms below. The installer brings
pam_rssh with it: a package where one exists, otherwise
built from a pinned, verified commit.
| Platform | Status | 
|---|---|
| Arch, Manjaro, EndeavourOS | ✅ tested end to end in CI | 
| Debian 12 / 13, Ubuntu 24.04, Mint, Pop!_OS | ✅ tested end to end in CI | 
| Fedora, RHEL / Rocky / Alma 9 | ✅ tested end to end in CI | 
| openSUSE Tumbleweed | ✅ tested end to end in CI | 
| Windows, via WSL (any distribution above) | 🧪 should work, untested; discovery may not see the phone across WSL2's NAT, so pass --phone | 
| macOS 14+ (via /etc/pam.d/sudo_local) | 🧪 experimental, untested | 
| FreeBSD ( security/pam_rssh port) | 🧪 experimental, untested | 
"Tested end to end" means every push runs tools/test/e2e.sh in a fresh
container of that distribution: the installer, pam_rssh and a real sudo, against a mock
phone. sudo must pass with no password while the phone approves, fall back to the password when
it denies, and be restored byte for byte by rollback.
Phone and host on the same LAN, with the phone at a stable address (a DHCP reservation).

A new authentication tool allows Linux users to approve sudo commands by using their Android phone's fingerprint sensor to sign requests securely over a local area network.

### Key Points
- The system utilizes the Android TEE or StrongBox to ensure biometric data and private keys never leave the mobile device.
- Authentication is handled via the pam_rssh module, which communicates with the phone over a local network using the ssh-agent protocol.
- If the phone is unavailable, denied, or times out after 60 seconds, the system automatically reverts to a standard password prompt.
- The solution requires Android 11 or higher with a Class 3 "strong" biometric sensor and supports major Linux distributions including Arch, Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora.
- Security is maintained by requiring a fresh biometric signature for every request, preventing malware from signing without physical user interaction.

### Why it Matters
This integration offers a more convenient and secure alternative to traditional password-based sudo authentication by leveraging hardware-backed mobile biometrics. By keeping all sensitive operations local and offline, it provides a robust security layer that enhances workflow efficiency without introducing cloud-based vulnerabilities.

articles.title: Fabio Alessandro Locati: SOPS for Ansible
articles.author: fale
articles.content:
SOPS for Ansible
 October 24, 2026
I’ve used Ansible for more than 10 years, and one problem I’ve seen everyone deal with is handling secrets in Ansible. Many people put them in the code, but since Ansible code often ends up in Git, that means adding secrets to Git repositories, which you should avoid at all costs.
Ansible Vault is a good solution, since it lets you encrypt files. I’ve used Ansible Vault for many years, but I think it has 2 major limitations.
The first limitation of Ansible Vault is that it uses AES, a symmetric encryption algorithm. Symmetric encryption uses a single key to encrypt and decrypt content. This means you need to provide the key at runtime, so Ansible Vault reduces the secrets issue but doesn’t solve it, because you still have to decide how to handle the master key securely.
The second limitation with Ansible Vault is that it encrypts at the file level, so if you open the file, you will just see random characters, This means that you will often end up having 2 files for variables, one for non-secret ones and the other for secret ones. The double file is not the real problem, though. The real problem is that the secret file contains both the encrypted value and the keys, so without the master key, you can’t read the keys. This means you need to document the key names elsewhere so you can modify the code without opening the Vault file.
Lately, I’ve started using CNCF’s SOPS project instead of Ansible Vault, since it solves both issues. In fact, SOPS encrypts at the YAML-file level, so it scrambles only the values while the keys remain clear. Also, it supports asymmetric encryption with a big number of providers.
Since I’ve used GPG keys for more than a decade, I have many workflows that leverage them, so it was an easy decision to use them for SOPS as well. You can also start with Age if you are not bought into the GPG ecosystem.
SOPS is managed with a .sops.yaml file in the root of the repository.
Mine look like this:
creation_rules:
  - path_regex: .*\.sops\.yaml$
    encrypted_regex: '^(.*_password|.*_secret|.*_key|.*_token)$'
    pgp: D880521E8D13FB5D0BCFC65817DBA3103879E9D9
This means that every file in the project that ends in .sops.yaml will have any value whose key ends in _password, _secret, _key, or _token encrypted with my GPG key.
It is possible to encrypt an unencrypted file with sops --encrypt group_vars/all/secrets.yaml > group_vars/all/secrets.sops.yaml.
SOPS will create the new file with the encrypted keys.
It is important to know that SOPS adds a structure called sops to the file where it saves its own configurations, and part of this configuration is a hash of the file, so any further modification to the file has to be done using the sops edit command; otherwise it will complain about data integrity being broken.
Ansible, by itself, can’t leverage SOPS secrets.
You’ll therefore need to tweak your ansible.cfg file to have:
[defaults]
vars_plugins_enabled = host_group_vars,community.sops.sops
If you already have a [default] group, you should simply add to it.
Further, you should add the community.sops collection to your requirements.yaml, so that it looks like:
collections:
  - name: community.sops
It is now possible to get the needed collections with:
ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yaml
From this point forward, SOPS variables will be usable exactly like any other variable.
It is important to remember that SOPS handles the security of the variables at rest, but Ansible will handle them at runtime, so it is important to keep all the Ansible good practices on secret management in mind, such as using no_log: true where there is a risk of variables ending up in logs, avoiding the use of ansible.builtin.debug or other modules that will leak the content of variables, etc.
I think SOPS is a very good secret store for Ansible. Although it has capabilities that would let it scale to big teams, I think different designs would be better for those scenarios. Personally, I use it for single-user projects, so I’m not hitting any of those limitations, and I can clearly see that a small team wouldn’t either.

Adopting SOPS improves developer experience by allowing teams to track encrypted secrets in version control without obscuring the structure of configuration files. This approach reduces the operational risks associated with managing symmetric master keys while maintaining compatibility with existing Ansible workflows.

articles.title: Wall St Week Ahead: Earnings flood, Fed meeting will test rickety AI market rally
articles.author: Reuters
articles.content:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Weakness in technology shares left investors on edge about the state of the AI trade that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary.
The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss on Friday, a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest daily drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta and Lam Research. Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners.
Three other hyperscalers -- Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon -- headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets.
"There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro.
"Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain."
Hyperscalers on the hot seat
Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict.
With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32% from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season.
"I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings."
Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays.
Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs.
"Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management.
Fed expected to pause on rates, for now
Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade.
Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar.
The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than 10% chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data.
One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections.
However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting a roughly 80% probability of such a move then.
Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision.
"Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike," Todd said.

articles.title: YouTuber escapes the modern AI tech market by recreating his 1996 PC
articles.author: editors@tomshardware.com (Bruno Ferreira) , Bruno Ferreira
articles.content:
These days, it's exceedingly difficult not to be jaded and weary about the tech market. Memory, graphics cards, and now storage are becoming impossible to obtain; there's basically no new consumer hardware being released; and there's AI everywhere. Technology YouTuber TrashBench (TB), too, is tired and was harkening back to the halcyon days when everything was fresh and straightforward — so he went back in time with a retro build.
More specifically, he recreated a facsimile of the first machine his parents bought him in 1996 when he was a wee lad, to play The Need for Speed: Special Edition — a PC-improved version of the first ever game in the series. According to the man, it was thanks to this machine that he fell in love with computers in general.
TB kicked things off with an Intel Pentium MMX 200 MHz CPU sitting atop an Epox Pronix EP-P55-BT motherboard, boasting what was at the time a new, fresh, convenient ZIF (Zero Insertion Force) socket. This motherboard popped up during the RAM transition from SIMM to DIMM, which is why you'll see two slots of each on the top. 32 MB of RAM went right in, a generous amount for the year.
Funnily enough, the CPU barely needed cooling, which is why a simple 40-mm fan suffices, although anyone who's lived through this era will tell you that those were guaranteed to start whining after just a few months of heavy usage. There is no case cooling, as it's just not needed.
However, he did need to correctly set the motherboard's jumpers, as such luxuries like automatically detecting CPU speed and voltage were just becoming normal. Yes, this meant that you could burn out a CPU if you played the jumper game wrong.
For graphics card duty, he enlisted an S3 Trio32 card, which was pretty, ahem, modest even in the era, and had no 3D rendering capabilities whatsoever. In this era, the now-ubiquitous 3D accelerator cards were just coming into fashion, and he eventually replaced the S3 with a Matrox Mystique 3D, another offering of dubious quality. Yet those were happy days, as any form of 3D acceleration was far better than none.
Storage comes by way of a Western Digital Caviar 22100 hard drive with a whopping two gigabytes of storage and the uncanny ability to emulate the dulcet tones of a jackhammer. TB eventually swapped it later for a roomier 80 GB unit. Again, due to the idiosyncrasies and constant transitions of the era — hardware doubled in speed and capacity nearly every year — he had to set a jumper to clip it to the likely amounts of either 8.4 GB or 33.4 GB, as the addressing space of BIOSes and disk controllers of the time were limited.

The build wraps up with an OG Sound Blaster 16 sound card and a CD-ROM drive. After test-driving the machine with Need for Speed, he moved on to Microsoft Flight Simulator 98, which necessitated a joystick. Naturally, he got the much-beloved Quickshot QS-123, a staple in many home PCs, and one that needed replacement in about six months, as its build quality matched its price.

Tech YouTuber TrashBench recreates his childhood 1996 PC build to revisit the era of early gaming, highlighting the technical challenges and simplicity of mid-nineties hardware configurations.

### Key Points
- The build features an Intel Pentium MMX 200 MHz CPU on an Epox Pronix EP-P55-BT motherboard with 32 MB of RAM.
- Graphics were handled by an S3 Trio32 card, later upgraded to a Matrox Mystique 3D for basic 3D acceleration.
- Storage relied on a noisy 2 GB Western Digital Caviar 22100 hard drive, which required manual jumper settings to manage BIOS capacity limits.
- The system utilized a Sound Blaster 16 sound card and a Quickshot QS-123 joystick for titles like Need for Speed and Microsoft Flight Simulator 98.
- Manual configuration of motherboard jumpers was required to set CPU speed and voltage, a common but risky task during that hardware generation.

### Why it Matters
This retro project highlights a growing consumer desire for the simplicity and ownership associated with early computing hardware. It reflects a broader cultural pushback against modern tech industry practices, such as telemetry, subscription models, and perceived predatory consumer exploitation.
